title_guess: Stock of money and the monetary aggregates M0 to M4: components, shares, why money is split by liquidity, narrow vs broad money
recurring_cast: stock-of-money card: yellow panel with a row of green banknotes, titled 'Stock of / money in our economy'
component tree: four blue headers (currency in circulation, deposits with RBI, banks, postal), each split into two light-blue boxes; the same boxes later become the column headers of the tick table
table_grid: rows M0-M4 against the eight component columns, filled with green ticks
person (blue father figure and black child figure in the analogy)
running_examples: shares written under the boxes: currency in circulation 95% with the public, 5% cash with banks; deposits with RBI 90% bankers', 10% other; banks and post office each about 15% demand and 85% time deposits
ranking badges: 1 = banks' time deposits, 2 = public's physical cash, 3 = banks' demand deposits
analogy: a father's monthly allowance cut from 10,000 to 3,000 rupees; last month's bill sorted into yearly, monthly, weekly and daily expenses
aggregates as ticked rows: M0, M1, M2 = M1 + postal DD, M3 = M1 + bank TD, M4 = M3 + all postal deposits (NSC excluded)

best_moments.why: M2's row first copies M1's ticks as the voice says 'on top of M1', then one extra tick lands on postal DD when that part is named; M3 and M4 repeat the move. 'Aggregate = earlier aggregate + one part' is seen as copy-the-row-and-add-a-tick

one stock-of-money card drops four headers and each header splits into two boxes as it is named; the same eight boxes are reused later as the table's column headers, so the parts never have to be relearned
numbered rank badges (1, 2, 3) pop under the boxes that hold the most money while the narrator answers his own question; this ranking is what later makes the time-deposit column matter
the banks' time-deposit column lights up yellow down the whole table when narrow money is said to leave it out: the narrow/broad dividing line is one coloured column

in the analogy a short bill grows into a long expense list and colour bands sort it into yearly, monthly, weekly and daily, one band per spoken word: sorting a mixed whole by type, shown on the object itself
final screen pairs the tick table with a falling 'liquidity' line over M1, M2, M3, M4: the order of liquidity read off a slope

weak_moments.why: why we split money into aggregates is a chain of four sentence boxes (liquidity differs, so segregated, helps economists and central banks, facilitates policy) with no picture of liquidity at all

the voice says the non-essential expenses can now be struck out, but no expense is ever struck; the analogy is then left without a drawn bridge to liquidity (the switch back happens inside a 15 s transcript gap, 285.8-300.7)

verify before reuse: a grey NOTE says financial assets such as gold and stock-market investment and, as far as the keyframe can be read, 'is considered' part of money supply, while the narrator says such money is NOT counted
verify before reuse: shares (95/5, 90/10, 15/85) are shown with no date or source, the post office is given the same 15/85 split as banks, and the 5% is only called 'negligible' in speech
narrow and broad money are defined in small paragraph boxes beside a shrunken table (about 110 words on screen); the definitions are read, not shown

segments.teaches: recall of the previous video: RBI creates reserve money (M0), also called high powered, basic, primary money or monetary base; through the money multiplier it becomes the money in our economy, whose stock is measured by four monetary aggregates M1-M4

elements.what: RBI emblem coin at the far left
green banknote labelled 'Reserve Money' with a big M0 title above
light-blue funnel / horn shape widening to the right, labelled 'Money Multiplier'
row of four green banknotes after the funnel, later boxed as 'Money in our economy' and then 'Stock of'
dotted line down from reserve money to a list of its four other names
dial weighing scale labelled 'Measure' pushing an arrow up into the money row, '4 monetary aggregates' under it
four chips M1 M2 M3 M4

segments.notes: 8 change events (~every 5 s). Transcript gap 14.8-28.3 s: the scale and 'Stock of' title appear while no words were recognised. The funnel widening from one note to four is a cheap 'multiplier' picture.
segments.idea: a small base of RBI money is multiplied into the economy's money stock, and that stock is measured in four aggregates
segments.shown_as: RBI coin feeds one green note labelled reserve money (M0); an arrow runs through a widening 'money multiplier' funnel and comes out as a row of four notes boxed as money in our economy; reserve money's other names list below; a weighing scale pushes up into the money row with '4 monetary aggregates' and chips M1-M4 under it

segments.teaches: the stock of money has four components (currency in circulation, deposits with RBI, money with banks, money with post offices), each with two parts (public cash / banks' cash; bankers' / other deposits with RBI; demand / time deposits at banks and at the post office); gold and shares are left out

elements.what: stock-of-money card moves to top centre with a long black bar under it
four down-arrows to blue headers: currency in circulation, deposits with RBI, banks, postal
grey NOTE box at lower left about gold and stock-market investment and money supply (on screen about 10 s)
green elbow connectors split each header into two light-blue boxes: [public] physical cash / cash with banks; bankers' deposits / other deposits with RBI; DD / TD under banks; DD / TD under postal

segments.notes: 12 change events (~every 7.5 s); each header lands within a second of its name. Verify the NOTE: the narrator says gold and stock-market money are not counted, the note's wording seems to say they are.
segments.idea: all the money in the economy sits in eight places, grouped into four components
segments.shown_as: the money card slides to the top and a bar draws under it; four arrows drop to four blue headers, one per spoken component; each header then splits by green elbow lines into two pale boxes as the narrator names the two kinds, ending in an eight-box tree

segments.teaches: where the money is concentrated: 95% of currency is cash with the public; 90% of RBI deposits are banks'; about 85% of bank and post-office money is in time deposits; ranking: banks' TD first, public cash second, banks' DD third

elements.what: small green down-arrows under each box ending in a share: 95%, 5%, 90%, 10%, 15%, 85%, 15%, 85%
black round rank badges 1 (banks TD), 2 (public cash), 3 (banks DD)

segments.notes: 5 detected change events (smaller ones missed; ~every 14 s). Shares are text under boxes; box sizes do not change with the share. No date or source for the shares.
segments.idea: most of India's money sits in banks' time deposits, then in cash with people, then in banks' demand deposits
segments.shown_as: a short green arrow drops under each of the eight boxes and a percentage writes on as it is spoken; then numbered black badges 1, 2, 3 pop under banks' TD, public cash and banks' DD as the narrator answers 'where is most money?'
segments.example: 95/5 currency, 90/10 RBI deposits, 15/85 DD/TD at banks and post offices; ranks 1-2-3

segments.teaches: knowing where money sits matters because RBI makes monetary policy on that basis; but there is a problem

elements.what: the tree folds into a compact header table inside the yellow money card; shares and badges vanish
down-arrow from the card to the RBI coin, then to a 'monetary policy formulate' label
RBI emblem coin
red 'PROBLEM' stamp landing on the arrow

segments.notes: 4 change events in 15 s. The stamp is a reusable 'problem' marker that returns later.
segments.idea: the picture of where money sits is the input RBI uses for policy, but using it raw is a problem
segments.shown_as: the eight-box tree compresses into a neat header table inside the money card; an arrow drops to the RBI coin and on to 'monetary policy formulate'; a red PROBLEM stamp thumps onto the arrow as 'problem' is said

segments.teaches: analogy: if your monthly allowance is cut from 10,000 to 3,000 rupees, last month's bill alone cannot tell you what to cut, because it mixes yearly, one-time, weekly and daily costs; listing and sorting expenses by how often they come lets you cut the right ones

elements.what: red PROBLEM stamp at top left
blue standing figure (father) at left and a small black figure (you) at right
arrow from father to child carrying '10000 ₹'
10000 ₹ struck, '3000 ₹' written above
paper bill with lines and a ₹ total, which grows into a tall expense list
colour bands on the list with tags Yearly (yellow), Monthly (blue), Weekly (pink), Daily (red-brown)

segments.notes: 7 change events (~every 11 s). The bands appear about 1.5-2 s before each spoken frequency word. Spoken 'strike out' of needless expenses is never shown; the screen returns to the money card at 293.6 inside a transcript gap (285.8-300.7).
segments.idea: a mixed pile can only be judged after it is sorted by type; the same is true for the money stock
segments.shown_as: under a PROBLEM stamp a blue father sends an arrow of 10,000 rupees to a small child figure; the amount is struck and 3,000 written above; a short bill appears beside the child, stretches into a long list of expenses, and coloured bands wipe over it from top to bottom labelled yearly, monthly, weekly, daily
segments.example: allowance 10,000 → 3,000 rupees a month; expenses yearly / monthly / weekly / daily

segments.teaches: the components of the stock of money differ in liquidity, so the stock is split into four monetary aggregates M1-M4; this helps economists, policymakers and the central bank analyse and monitor money supply and make policy

elements.what: the money card with its compact eight-box header table, PROBLEM stamp below it
text box 'liquidity of each component differs' → down-arrow → 'stock of money is segregated into aggregates'
chips M1 M2 M3 M4
sentence: segregation helps economists, policymakers and central banks analyse and monitor money supply
arrow to 'facilitates policy decisions'

segments.notes: 7 change events (~every 5 s). Pure sentence chain; 'liquidity' is never drawn (no tap, no lock, no speed).
segments.idea: because the parts are not equally spendable, money is measured in separate aggregates, which guides policy
segments.shown_as: the money card returns with its PROBLEM stamp; below it a box says each part's liquidity differs, an arrow drops to 'segregated into aggregates', chips M1-M4 pop in, then a sentence about better analysis and monitoring writes on with an arrow to 'facilitates policy decisions'

segments.teaches: how each aggregate is built from the eight parts: M0 = currency in circulation + all deposits with RBI; M1 = public cash + other deposits with RBI + banks' DD; M2 = M1 + postal DD; M3 = M1 + banks' TD; M4 = M3 + postal DD and TD

elements.what: the eight component boxes become column headers; rows M0, M1, M2, M3, M4 in pale green with yellow side cells
green ticks filling each row cell by cell as parts are named

segments.notes: 8 change events (~every 8 s). Each new row first copies the ticks of the aggregate it is built on, then adds the new part's tick. The M3 row has no postal-DD tick while M2 does, so the table quietly shows M3 is not 'M2 + something' (a common learner trap, never said aloud).
segments.idea: each monetary aggregate is a chosen set of the eight parts, and the bigger ones are built on smaller ones
segments.shown_as: the header boxes slide up to become columns and five rows M0-M4 draw under them; green ticks pop into M0's row on currency and on RBI deposits; M1 ticks public cash, other deposits and banks' DD; each later row copies the row it is built on as 'on top of M1/M3' is said, then the extra tick lands on postal DD, banks' TD, or both postal boxes
segments.example: M2 = M1 + postal DD; M3 = M1 + bank TD; M4 = M3 + postal DD + postal TD

segments.teaches: M0 is reserve money, the base and source of all money; M1 and M2 are narrow money, most liquid and ready for transactions, because banks' time deposits are left out; M3 and M4 are broad money because they include them; in banking, money supply means M3, and more M3 lets banks lend more; NSCs are not in M4

elements.what: tick table shrinks to the right-centre
RESERVE MONEY heading and box (base level of money supply) joined by a line to the M0 row, with arrows to 'other names' and 'source of all other money' boxes
NARROW MONEY box (most liquid, readily available for transactions) with two connector dots to M1 and M2
banks' TD column shaded yellow down the table
BROAD MONEY box (broader, less liquid than M1) joined to M3 and M4, with arrows to 'M3 is money supply' and 'banks lend more when broad money is more'
'Excludes National Savings Certificates' tag pointing at M4's postal ticks

segments.notes: 9 change events (~every 8 s). Three side panels of sentence boxes; screen ends near 110 words. The yellow TD column is the one picture-level cue for narrow vs broad.
segments.idea: the aggregates fall into three families: base money (M0), narrow money (M1, M2) and broad money (M3, M4), split by whether banks' time deposits are in
segments.shown_as: the tick table shrinks; a reserve-money box hooks onto the M0 row with arrows to its other names and 'source of all money'; a narrow-money box hooks onto M1 and M2; the banks' TD column glows yellow down the table; a broad-money box hooks onto M3 and M4 with arrows to 'M3 = money supply' and 'more broad money, more lending'; a small tag on M4's postal ticks says NSCs are excluded

segments.teaches: liquidity is highest in M1 and falls through M2, M3 to M4; recap of the formulas M2 = M1 + post-office savings deposits, M3 = M1 + bank time deposits, M4 = M3 + all post-office deposits except NSC

elements.what: clean tick table at left
y-axis 'liquidity', x-axis M1 M2 M3 M4 chips; a straight falling line with dotted drop lines
three lines: M2 = M1 + ..., M3 = M1 + ..., M4 = M3 + ...

segments.notes: 2 change events in 15 s. The graph has no numbers; it is an order, not data.
segments.idea: the wider the aggregate, the less liquid it is
segments.shown_as: the canvas resets to the tick table with a small graph at right: a line slopes down over M1, M2, M3, M4 on a 'liquidity' axis; three formula lines write under the table
segments.example: M2 = M1 + post-office savings; M3 = M1 + bank TD; M4 = M3 + post-office deposits (not NSC)
